units.title: Stablecoin-native L1s
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Known weaknesses. Collect security advisories, audit reports, bug bounty write-ups, incident post-mortems and open issues for this network's execution client, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years, including behaviour the network calls by design. For each, decide whether an ordinary account could use it against funds in the PoolManager.

code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read. Leads L-603, L-608, L-609 and L-599. On Monad a frequently called contract runs as native code that the client's compiler emits, and simulated calls on the RPC always use the interpreter, so the compiled multiplication paths have been tested only through mined swaps. Two earlier readers left them unread, and a verifier of cycle 9 showed that the PoolManager bytecode contains MULMOD with the literal moduli 2^96 and 2^128 (program counters 22378 and 22639 of the runtime; confirm and list every MULMOD and MUL site with a literal operand, with the source line each implements, using cycles/009/core-code-bytecode-map.work). Read the Monad source at tag v0.16.5 (a copy is in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v4-core/0b315df9-4a6b-5032-a881-24bad3c79fc5/scratchpad/opsrc-monad/v0165/ ; fetch missing files from raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/v0.16.5/<path>): category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.cpp, the functions mul_mod2, mul_with_bit_size, mul_optimized and the MulEmitter class (about lines 6272 to 7040 and 7990 to 8090), and the EXP code generation. Transcribe each into Python at the level of the emitted instructions (64 bit limbs, carries, which limbs are computed and which are skipped, the masks) for every operand location the emitter distinguishes (general registers, stack offsets, AVX registers, literals, and the same slot used for both operands). Run the transcriptions against Python integers for: mulmod(a, b, 2^96) and mulmod(a, b, 2^128) with a and b random, with all limbs set, with low limbs zero, with one operand below 2^128 and the other above; the 19 literal multipliers of TickMath.getSqrtPriceAtTick (src/libraries/TickMath.sol), the first-step select of that function, the signed multiply by 255738958999603826347141 in getTickAtSqrtPrice, the multiplications inside FullMath.mulDiv (including the six inverse steps), and every other MUL with a literal in the bytecode. At least a million cases per path. Then say, for each path, which mined results on Monad already exercise it (research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/swaps.py and rounding.py read Swap events and check them against the source's math; 17,434 swaps passed) and which path no mined result can show. Report any operand for which the emitted code differs from the specification, with the exact bytes of the PoolManager that would trigger it and the pool state needed. Do not claim a fault from reading alone: show the transcription and the failing operands, and say how to confirm it from mined transactions without sending one. Also check the release notes and the emitter diff of v0.16.6 and v0.16.7 for changes to these functions.

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read. Leads L-606, L-607, L-610 and L-601. MegaETH (chain id 4326, RPC https://mainnet.megaeth.com/rpc, PoolManager 0xacb7e78fa05d562e0a5d3089ec896d57d057d38e) reports mega-reth/v2.2.3, whose source is not public. Part one: which executor produces mainnet blocks and which one answers eth_call: the mega-evm interpreter (megaeth-labs/mega-evm, revm based), an ahead-of-time or just-in-time compiler (megaeth-labs/evmone-compiler, revmc or another), and does the stateless validator use the same one? Use the public repositories, docs.megaeth.com, release notes and engineering posts. Part two: whatever the answer, test the block producer through mined results, because simulated calls may use another path. research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/swaps.py, replay.py and rounding.py check Swap events of the PoolManager against the source's math (39,074 swaps passed the tick relation); extend this on MegaETH to (a) all swaps that crossed ticks, by full replay, (b) swaps at negative ticks and near the ends of the tick range, (c) transactions in which a frame that entered PoolManager.unlock reverted and a later frame of the same transaction completed an unlock, and transactions in which settle or a swap ran inside a reverted inner frame (on-chain quoters revert after a swap): did the block producer roll back transient storage and storage as the specification requires? Read the receipts and events; use debug or trace methods if the endpoint serves them. Part three: which per-frame resource limits of the MegaETH execution rules (compute gas, data size, key-value updates, state growth, and the cap on gas after reading block data or the oracle) can make a PoolManager call return a different result than on Ethereum for the same input, as opposed to failing as a whole: is there any limit whose breach is caught inside the PoolManager's own frame so that execution continues with a failed subcall? Measure with the scripts of tools/opdiff where that helps. Part four: is the Rex6 rule set active on mainnet, and what does it change for the instruction set.

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read. Leads L-611 and L-591. A reader of cycle 9 reported that the Go toolchain go1.27.3, which the Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain nodes report in web3_clientVersion, and go1.26.10, which the BNB Smart Chain node reports, are affected by a dead-store miscompile filed as Go issue 81863: a store through a pointer that a branch selected between the addresses of two local variables can be dropped. Part one: confirm the issue from the primary source (the Go issue tracker and release notes: which versions are affected, on which architectures, which code shape triggers it, in which release it is fixed) and say exactly which toolchain each go-ethereum family node of the 21 networks reports today: Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium (nitro), BNB Smart Chain (bsc), Polygon (bor), Avalanche (avalanchego), and the op-geth backend of Celo's endpoint. Part two: search the code that computes opcode results and state for the triggering shape: holiman/uint256 at v1.3.2 and v1.2.4 (all of uint256.go, mod.go, div and the helpers udivrem, umul, reduce4, the Lsh and Rsh families, ExtendSign, SDiv, SMod), and core/vm (instructions.go, interpreter.go, stack.go, memory.go, the transient storage and journal code in core/state) of the nitro go-ethereum fork at 0e44603, bsc v1.8.2, bor v2.11.1 and libevm. Sources: raw.githubusercontent.com with curl; copies of several are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v4-core/0b315df9-4a6b-5032-a881-24bad3c79fc5/scratchpad/opsrc-bsc and opsrc-nitro. List every function with the shape and say whether a dropped store there would change an opcode result, with the operands that would show it. Part three: for each such operand run the vectors against the live endpoints with research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py shows how a dispatcher contract is placed by state override), pairing each request with web3_clientVersion so that the build that answered is known, on both arm64 and amd64 builds where both exist. Report every network whose node runs an affected toolchain, whether any affected function is on the path of an opcode the PoolManager bytecode uses, and the result of the vectors.
